summary: A periodic snapshot from the Internet Architecture Board listing the standardization state of Internet protocols at the time. It served as a catalog of which protocols were standards and how mature they were. The series is now historic, and this edition was replaced by RFC 2500.

eli5.summary: Think of a school report card listing every protocol and how far along each one is. This is one old copy of that report card, and newer ones replaced it.

questions: what are the internet official protocol standards
how do internet protocols become standards
subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's updated list of Internet protocol standards for late 1998.

tldr.problem: The state of Internet protocols changes frequently as new ones are developed and old ones are retired, so the community needs a regularly updated official list.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board publishes a periodic snapshot categorizing all protocols by maturity level (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Informational, Historic) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended).
tldr.outcome: RFC 2400 superseded RFC 2300 just four months after it was published (May to September 1998), documenting additional new protocols and status changes. It too is now Historic, replaced by RFC 2500.

today: RFC 2400 is Historic, superseded by RFC 2500. Modern sources for Internet protocol standards are the IETF website and the RFC Editor site, which maintain living documents rather than periodic snapshots. The standardization process described here remains the foundation for Internet standards but is now managed through different mechanisms.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) maintains the authoritative list of standards for Internet protocols, working through the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and its steering group, the IESG. The RFC explains the multistate maturity process: new protocols start as Proposed Standards, advance to Draft Standards after at least two implementations and six months of review, and finally become Standards when they demonstrate operational interoperability.

The RFC also defines the role of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) for experimental work and emphasizes that the Internet standards process, described in detail in RFC 2026, is the method the IAB recommends for ensuring interoperability across the Internet. While some vendor or research protocols gain widespread use outside this process, the IAB recommends using the official process to prevent incompatibility.
sections.eli5: Internet protocols go through a strict approval process: first Proposed (maybe it will work), then Draft (we are testing it), then Standard (it is official). The Internet Architecture Board oversees this to make sure everyone is on the same page.

sections.title: Maturity Levels and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Every protocol is assigned two independent categories. Maturity level reflects the standardization state: Standard (officially approved by IESG), Draft Standard (actively considered, substantial testing needed), Proposed Standard (candidate for standardization, implementation desired), Experimental (research work only, not for general use), Informational (published from other standards bodies or for reference), or Historic (superseded or out of use).

Requirement level indicates what systems should do: Required (all systems must implement), Recommended (systems should implement), Elective (optional), Limited Use (for specific circumstances only), or Not Recommended (avoid using). The RFC includes a matrix showing that most Standards are either Recommended or Elective, while Experimental protocols are typically Limited Use.
sections.eli5: Every protocol gets two grades: one for how official it is (Standard, Draft, Proposed, Experimental, Informational, or Historic) and one for what you should do with it (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, or Not Recommended).

sections.title: Understanding Each Category
sections.content:
Standard Protocols are officially approved and receive STD numbers. Draft Standard protocols are under active IESG consideration with substantial testing required; the community may see changes before standardization. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates for eventual standardization; multiple independent implementations are desirable.

Experimental protocols should only be implemented by researchers who coordinate with the protocol developer, as they are not intended for general deployment. Informational protocols come from other standards bodies, vendors, or are published for the Internet community's reference. Historic protocols are unlikely to ever become standards, either because better protocols have superseded them or community interest has faded.
sections.eli5: Standard is official, Draft is being tested seriously, Proposed is a candidate, Experimental is for researchers only, Informational is from elsewhere, and Historic is obsolete.

sections.title: The Protocol Lists and Related Documents
sections.content:
The RFC lists protocols organized by their maturity level in sections 6.2 through 6.10, with section 6.1 describing recent changes (new protocols and status movements). The RFC also references three important companion documents: Assigned Numbers (RFC 1700), which lists protocol codes and parameter constants; Gateway Requirements (RFC 1812), which specifies requirements for IP routers; and Host Requirements (RFCs 1122 and 1123), which specify requirements for end systems.

The RFC notes that the reference standard for the Internet protocol suite was formerly RFC 2026, which defines the detailed standards process. It also mentions that DoD MIL-STD specifications are obsolete and references the DoD's Joint Technical Architecture for current approved standards lists.
sections.eli5: The bulk of the RFC is a big categorized list of all the protocols, plus references to more detailed documents about how to build routers and computers using these protocols.

sections.title: Edition and Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 2400 was published in September 1998 and superseded the May 1998 edition (RFC 2300), reflecting new protocols and status changes in just four months. The RFC is part of a periodic series, with new editions released roughly every 100 RFCs, and each edition supersedes all prior editions in the series going back decades.

Like its predecessor RFC 2300, RFC 2400 is now Historic: it was superseded by RFC 2500. The Internet community now maintains updated protocol standards lists on the Internet Engineering Task Force website and the RFC Editor's pages rather than relying on a single RFC document. Readers should always consult the most current source for protocol standardization status.
sections.eli5: This edition came out in September 1998, just a few months after RFC 2300. It is now old news, replaced by newer lists. For current protocol standards, check the IETF website.
